Let \(\rho>0\), and let \(S\) be a real-valued real-analytic function on \((-\rho,\rho)^2\), with Taylor expansion
\[
S(x,y)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\geq0}c_{\alpha,\beta}x^\alpha y^\beta.
\]
Assume that at least one coefficient with \(\alpha,\beta\geq1\) is nonzero. Define its reduced Newton polyhedron by
\[
N_r(S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{\substack{\alpha,\beta\geq1\\c_{\alpha,\beta}\ne0}}\bigl((\alpha,\beta)+[0,\infty)^2\bigr)\right).
\]
Let \(\mathcal V\) be the set of vertices of \(N_r(S)\), and denote the vertices with smallest and largest first coordinate by \((A_L,B_L)\) and \((A_R,B_R)\), respectively; these may coincide.

For \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty((-\rho,\rho)^3)\), define
\[
R_\varphi f(t,x)=\int_{-\rho}^{\rho}f(t+S(x,y),y)\varphi(t,x,y)\,dy
\]
when \(|x|<\rho\), and set it equal to zero otherwise. Use the Bessel-potential Sobolev norm
\[
\|g\|_{L_s^p(\mathbb R^2)}=\left\|\mathcal F^{-1}\!\left[(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{s/2}\widehat g(\xi)\right]\right\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)},
\qquad \widehat g(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-2\pi i z\cdot\xi}g(z)\,dz.
\]
For each \((a,b)\in\partial N_r(S)\), put
\[
p(a,b)=\frac{a+b}{a},\qquad s(a,b)=\frac1{a+b}.
\]
Call \((a,b)\) locally admissible if there exists \(\varepsilon\in(0,\rho)\) such that, for every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)^3)\) satisfying \(\varphi(0,0,0)\ne0\), there is a finite constant \(C_\varphi\), independent of \(f\), for which
\[
\|R_\varphi f\|_{L_{s(a,b)}^{p(a,b)}(\mathbb R^2)}\leq C_\varphi\|f\|_{L^{p(a,b)}(\mathbb R^2)}
\quad\text{for every }f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2).
\]
Determine the exact exceptional set
\[
\mathcal E(S)=\{(a,b)\in\partial N_r(S):(a,b)\text{ is not locally admissible}\}
\]
as an explicit formula in \(\mathcal V,A_L,B_L,A_R,B_R\), including all endpoint inclusion conventions.
</problem>

3	Put \(\Delta=\{(u,u):u\geq1\}\). Empty intervals in the formula below are to be omitted.
4	
5	Then the answer is
6	\[
7	\boxed{\begin{aligned}
8	\mathcal E(S)={}&(\mathcal V\setminus\Delta)\\
9	&{}\cup\{(A_L,b):B_L\leq b<A_L\}\\
10	&{}\cup\{(a,B_R):A_R\leq a<B_R\}.
11	\end{aligned}}\tag{1}
12	\]
13	
14	Thus:
15	
16	* every vertex off the diagonal is exceptional;
17	* every vertex on the diagonal is admissible;
18	* the relative interior of every compact edge is admissible;
19	* on either unbounded edge, the exceptional part, if nonempty, runs **from the end vertex, included, to the diagonal, excluded**.
20	
21	In particular, there are no exceptional points when the sole vertex is \((1,1)\).
22	
23	The proof uses standard Littlewood–Paley theory and the classical planar finite-type Sobolev theorem. I state precisely the version of that theorem being used, so that the analytic input, as well as the endpoint conventions, is explicit.
24	
25	## 1. Analytic estimates used in the proof
26	
27	Write \(J_t^s=(1-\partial_t^2)^{s/2}\). Changes in the Fourier normalization only change constants.
28	
29	Here are the two standard localized planar Radon estimates we need.
30	
31	### Nondegenerate estimate
32	
33	Suppose \(P\) and an amplitude are supported in fixed bounded coordinate boxes, their sufficiently many derivatives are bounded, and
34	\[
35	|P_{xy}|\geq c>0.
36	\]
37	For
38	\[
39	Tf(t,x)=\int f(t+P(x,y),y)a(x,y)\,dy,
40	\]
41	one has
42	\[
43	\|J_t^\sigma Tf\|_p\lesssim\|f\|_p,
44	\qquad
45	0\leq\sigma\leq\min(1/p,1/p').\tag{2}
46	\]
47	The constants are uniform under the indicated derivative bounds and lower bound. This is the usual nondegenerate Fourier-integral-operator Sobolev estimate.
48	
49	Its elementary, frequency-localized, strict version will also be useful. If \(P_n\) localizes the \(t\)-frequency to size \(2^n\), then, for every
50	\[
51	\theta<\min(1/p,1/p'),
52	\]
53	\[
54	\|TP_n\|_{p\to p}\lesssim (1+2^n)^{-\theta}.\tag{3}
55	\]
56	Indeed, interpolate the \(L^2\) oscillatory-integral bound with the elementary \(L^q\) bound, choosing \(q\) sufficiently close to \(1\) or \(\infty\).
57	
58	### Two-sided finite-type estimate
59	
60	Suppose \(m\geq1\), and on a fixed small coordinate box
61	\[
62	|\partial_x^m P_{xy}|\geq c,\qquad
63	|\partial_y^m P_{xy}|\geq c.
64	\]
65	The planar two-sided finite-type Sobolev theorem gives
66	\[
67	\|J_t^\sigma Tf\|_p\lesssim\|f\|_p \tag{4}
68	\]
69	if
70	\[
71	0\leq\sigma\leq
72	\min\left(\frac1p,\frac1{p'},\frac1{m+2}\right),
73	\]
74	except for the two corner cases
75	\[
76	(\sigma,p)=\left(\frac1{m+2},m+2\right),\qquad
77	\left(\frac1{m+2},\frac{m+2}{m+1}\right).\tag{5}
78	\]
79	We use the usual uniform localized form of this theorem: finitely many derivative bounds and the displayed lower bounds control the constant. This is the standard planar finite-type theorem for Radon transforms; in particular, this input is not a Newton-polygon endpoint assertion about arbitrary vertices.
80	
81	Smooth amplitudes, bounded families of amplitudes, and restriction to smaller boxes are allowed in (2)–(4).
82	
83	We also use two familiar localization facts:
84	
85	1. For a compactly supported Radon operator of this form,
86	   \[
87	   \|Rf\|_{L_s^p}\lesssim
88	   \|J_t^sRf\|_p+\|f\|_p. \tag{6}
89	   \]
90	   To see this, separate output frequencies into
91	   \(|\xi_x|\lesssim1+|\xi_t|\), where \(J_t^s\) controls the full Sobolev multiplier, and its complement. On the complement the \(x\)-phase is nonstationary, and integration by parts gives a smoothing operator.
92	2. A smooth compact amplitude can be expanded in a rapidly convergent Fourier series into separated amplitudes. The preceding estimates have at most polynomial dependence on the modulation parameters, so it suffices to prove the estimates with a \(t\)-independent amplitude and then localize in \(t\).
93	
94	These facts also justify the usual local-to-global argument in the \(t\) variable.
95	
96	## 2. Preliminary reductions
97	
98	Remove the pure terms of \(S\). More explicitly, write
99	\[
100	S(x,y)=P(x,y)+u(x)+v(y),\qquad
101	P(x,y)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\geq1}c_{\alpha,\beta}x^\alpha y^\beta.
102	\]
103	The input shear \((t,y)\mapsto(t+v(y),y)\) and output shear
104	\((t,x)\mapsto(t+u(x),x)\) remove \(u,v\). They preserve \(L^p\), commute with \(J_t^s\), and are bounded changes of variables on the localized full Sobolev spaces under consideration. They do not change the reduced Newton polyhedron.
105	
106	We may therefore assume
107	\[
108	S(x,0)=S(0,y)=0. \tag{7}
109	\]
110	
111	The set \(\mathcal V\) is finite and consists of integer points. This follows, for example, from the elementary fact that a subset of \(\mathbb N^2\) has only finitely many coordinatewise minimal elements.
112	
113	For \(j,k\geq1\), define
114	\[
115	H(j,k)=\min_{(A,B)\in\mathcal V}(Aj+Bk). \tag{8}
116	\]
117	For a proposed boundary point \((a,b)\), abbreviate
118	\[
119	s=\frac1{a+b},\qquad
120	\frac1p=as,\qquad \frac1{p'}=bs.
121	\]
122	The fundamental dyadic weight is
123	\[
124	W_{jk}=2^{sH(j,k)-j/p-k/p'}
125	      =2^{-s(aj+bk-H(j,k))}. \tag{9}
126	\]
127	Since \((a,b)\in N_r(S)\),
128	\[
129	0<W_{jk}\leq1. \tag{10}
130	\]
131	
132	## 3. The Newton decomposition and its transition pieces
133	
134	Decompose the punctured \(x,y\) neighborhood into signed dyadic rectangles
135	\[
136	|x|\asymp X=2^{-j},\qquad |y|\asymp Y=2^{-k}.
137	\]
138	
139	Choose a sufficiently large fixed integer \(M\). There are two kinds of rectangles.
140	
141	* **Vertex rectangles:** one vertex \((A,B)\) wins in (8), with a gap at least \(M\) from the other relevant vertices.
142	* **Transition rectangles:** \(j,k\) lie in a fixed-width strip about a normal ray to a compact edge.
143	
144	On a vertex rectangle, after setting
145	\[
146	x=Xu,\quad y=Yv,\quad D=2^{-H(j,k)},
147	\]
148	the normalized phase \(D^{-1}S(Xu,Yv)\) is uniformly close to a nonzero multiple of \(u^Av^B\). In particular its mixed derivative is bounded away from zero on the signed unit annuli.
149	
150	On a transition rectangle it is uniformly close to a rescaled compact-face polynomial.
151	
152	These assertions, including uniform bounds for any prescribed finite number of derivatives, follow directly from the convergent power series. Terms away from the selected face have an extra positive dyadic exponent; choose \(M\) large, then the original neighborhood small. The infinite tail is controlled by absolute convergence of the differentiated power series.
153	
154	We first dispose of all transition rectangles.
155	
156	Let a compact edge have endpoints
157	\[
158	(A,B),\quad(C,D),\qquad A<C,\quad B>D.
159	\]
160	Write
161	\[
162	C-A=\ell u,\qquad B-D=\ell v,\qquad
163	\gcd(u,v)=1.
164	\]
165	Here \(\ell,u,v\) are positive integers. The mixed derivative of the face polynomial is, up to a monomial factor, a degree-\(\ell\) polynomial in \(x^u/y^v\). Consequently every nonzero real root has multiplicity
166	\[
167	m\leq\ell. \tag{11}
168	\]
169	At such a root both the \(x\)- and \(y\)-derivatives of order \(m\) of the mixed derivative are nonzero: the root curve \(x^u=c\,y^v\) has nonzero derivatives in both directions on the signed annuli.
170	
171	Here is the numerical observation ensuring that (4) applies. The supporting line of this edge is
172	\[
173	v\alpha+u\beta=C_0,
174	\qquad
175	C_0=vA+uD+\ell uv.
176	\]
177	For any \((a,b)\in N_r(S)\), using \(a,b\geq1\),
178	\[
179	\begin{aligned}
180	\max(u,v)(a+b-2)
181	&\geq v(a-1)+u(b-1)\\
182	&\geq C_0-u-v\\
183	&\geq \ell uv.
184	\end{aligned}
185	\]
186	Thus
187	\[
188	a+b\geq 2+\ell\min(u,v)\geq m+2. \tag{12}
189	\]
190	
191	The two forbidden equalities in (5) would require
192	\[
193	(a,b)=(1,m+1)\quad\text{or}\quad(m+1,1).
194	\]
195	Equality throughout (12) then shows that the point is an endpoint of the compact edge. Unless \(m=0\), it is an off-diagonal vertex. Those points are among the proposed exceptions.
196	
197	Therefore, for every point not in (1), the finite-type theorem, or (2) away from the roots, applies on every transition rectangle. Scaling back gives its norm at most
198	\[
199	C X^{1/p}Y^{1/p'}D^{-s}=C W_{jk}. \tag{13}
200	\]
201	The transition rectangles lie in finitely many strips
202	\[
203	|k-qj|\leq C,\qquad 0<q<\infty.
204	\]
205	Each strip has uniformly bounded row and column counts. Since \(W_{jk}\leq1\), the discrete Schur test sums (13). This proves the required estimate for every transition contribution.
206	
207	## 4. Summation on vertex rectangles
208	
209	Assume first that
210	\[
211	a>1,\qquad b>1.
212	\]
213	Choose
214	\[
215	s<\theta<\min(1/p,1/p').
216	\]
217	For a vertex rectangle and a \(t\)-frequency band \(2^n\), (3), after scaling, gives
218	\[
219	\|R_{jk}P_n\|_{p\to p}
220	\lesssim
221	2^{-j/p-k/p'}\min\{1,2^{-\theta(n-H(j,k))}\}. \tag{14}
222	\]
223	After applying \(J_t^s\), its upper bound is
224	\[
225	C W_{jk}\,\omega(n-H(j,k)), \tag{15}
226	\]
227	where
228	\[
229	\omega(l)=
230	\begin{cases}
231	2^{sl},&l\leq0,\\
232	2^{-(\theta-s)l},&l>0.
233	\end{cases}
234	\qquad
235	\sum_{l\in\mathbb Z}\omega(l)<\infty. \tag{16}
236	\]
237	
238	It suffices to sum at one fixed offset
239	\[
240	n-H(j,k)=l. \tag{17}
241	\]
242	
243	Two elementary properties are useful:
244	
245	* \(H(j,k)\) increases by at least \(1\) when either integer coordinate increases by \(1\);
246	* for fixed \(j,n,l\), (17) has at most one \(k\), and for fixed \(k,n,l\), at most one \(j\).
247	
248	With smooth frequency cutoffs these counts become bounded absolute constants.
249	
250	We consider all possible admissible boundary locations.
251	
252	### 4.1 Relative interiors of compact edges
253	
254	Suppose \((a,b)\) is strictly between vertices \(V_0,V_1\). Then
255	\[
256	(a,b)=\tau V_0+(1-\tau)V_1,\qquad0<\tau<1.
257	\]
258	Since \(H\leq\min(V_0\cdot(j,k),V_1\cdot(j,k))\),
259	\[
260	aj+bk-H(j,k)
261	\geq
262	\min(\tau,1-\tau)\,
263	|(V_1-V_0)\cdot(j,k)|.
264	\]
265	Consequently \(W_{jk}\) has uniformly summable rows and columns.
266	
267	For a fixed \(l\), apply Littlewood–Paley theory in \(t\), the triangle inequality in its square-function space, and then the discrete Schur test to (15). This bounds the fixed-offset operator on \(L^p\). Summing (16) proves the estimate.
268	
269	### 4.2 Diagonal vertices
270	
271	Here \((a,b)=(d,d)\), so \(p=2\). At fixed \(l\), the two bounded-incidence properties following (17), together with \(W_{jk}\leq1\), give an \(L^2\) bound by orthogonality in \(t\) and bounded overlap of the spatial annuli.
272	
273	Summing (16) proves admissibility when \(d>1\). For \(d=1\), \(S_{xy}(0,0)\ne0\), and the full local result follows directly from (2).
274	
275	### 4.3 The horizontal unbounded edge
276	
277	Let
278	\[
279	b=B_R,\qquad a>A_R,\qquad a\geq b.
280	\]
281	Thus \(p\leq2\). From \(H(j,k)\leq A_Rj+bk\),
282	\[
283	W_{jk}\leq2^{-(a-A_R)sj}. \tag{18}
284	\]
285	
286	At a fixed \(j,l\), different \(k\)'s in (17) have different frequency bands. Since \(p\leq2\), the \(\ell^2\) square function is bounded by the \(\ell^p\) sum. Using (15), then disjointness of the input \(y\)-annuli, gives
287	\[
288	\|\text{output on the }j\text{-annulus}\|_p^p
289	\lesssim
290	2^{-p(a-A_R)sj}\|f\|_p^p.
291	\]
292	Now sum in \(j\), and then in \(l\). The strict inequality \(a>A_R\) makes (18) summable.
293	
294	This proves exactly the claimed admissible portion of this edge when \(b>1\).
295	
296	### 4.4 The vertical unbounded edge
297	
298	Transpose the operator and exchange \(x,y\). The preceding argument gives admissibility for
299	\[
300	a=A_L,\qquad b>B_L,\qquad b\geq a.
301	\]
302	
303	### 4.5 Boundary points with a coordinate equal to \(1\)
304	
305	Apart from \((1,1)\), an admissible boundary point with a coordinate \(1\) lies on one of the good unbounded rays. By transposition it suffices to consider
306	\[
307	b=B_R=1,\qquad a>A_R.
308	\]
309	Now \(s=1/p'\), so the strict choice of \(\theta\) used in (14) is unavailable.
310	
311	Choose a rational \(q>0\) sufficiently far inside the normal cone at the rightmost vertex. For each \(x\)-annulus \(X\), group together
312	\[
313	|y|\leq cX^q.
314	\]
315	Rescale this entire region with \(Y=cX^q\). Its normalized phase has mixed derivative uniformly bounded away from zero, including at \(y=0\): its leading \(y\)-term is a nonzero multiple of \(u^{A_R}v\). Apply the endpoint nondegenerate estimate (2). Its scaling factor is
316	\[
317	X^{1/p}Y^{1/p'}(X^{A_R}Y)^{-s}
318	=X^{(a-A_R)s}.
319	\]
320	These factors are summable over \(x\)-annuli.
321	
322	In the remaining vertex rectangles, \(k\leq qj+C\). Apply the full nondegenerate estimate separately to each rectangle. There are \(O(j+1)\) of them at a given \(j\), while their weights are bounded by the exponential in (18). Their sum converges. Transition rectangles were already treated in Section 3.
323	
324	This completes sufficiency for every point outside (1), including every claimed endpoint. By (6) and amplitude localization, the conclusion is precisely the full Bessel-potential estimate in the question, for all sufficiently small supported amplitudes.
325	
326	## 5. A randomized obstruction
327	
328	We next prove failure at every point in (1).
329	
330	We use the following standard consequence of Littlewood–Paley theory and Khintchine's inequality. Suppose functions \(F_\nu\) have separated \(t\)-frequencies \(\lambda_\nu\), and, on a fixed \(t\)-interval and an \(x\)-set \(E\),
331	\[
332	|\lambda_\nu^s RF_\nu|\geq cA
333	\quad(1\leq\nu\leq N).
334	\]
335	Then some choice of signs satisfies
336	\[
337	\left\|J_t^sR\Big(\sum_{\nu=1}^N\epsilon_\nu F_\nu\Big)\right\|_p
338	\gtrsim A\,|E|^{1/p}N^{1/2}. \tag{19}
339	\]
340	This also holds with smooth compact \(t\)-cutoffs. The frequency leakage from the cutoff is rapidly decreasing; taking sufficiently separated, sufficiently high frequencies makes its contribution smaller than half the right-hand side.
341	
342	We choose all cutoffs nonnegative and equal to \(1\) on the smaller sets used below.
343	
344	### 5.1 Vertices above the diagonal
345	
346	Let \((a,b)\in\mathcal V\), with \(b>a\). Thus
347	\[
348	p=\frac{a+b}{a}>2.
349	\]
350	
351	Because this point is a vertex, there is a nonempty open interval of positive \(q\)'s on which
352	\[
353	a+qb<A+qB
354	\quad\text{for every other }(A,B)\in\mathcal V. \tag{20}
355	\]
356	Choose a closed subinterval of that interval.
357	
358	Let \(X\downarrow0\). There are \(N\asymp\log(1/X)\) separated dyadic numbers \(Y_\nu\) whose logarithmic slopes lie in that subinterval. On
359	\[
360	x\asymp X,\qquad y\asymp Y_\nu,
361	\]
362	analyticity and (20) give, uniformly,
363	\[
364	S(x,y)=c_{a,b}x^ay^b+o(X^aY_\nu^b). \tag{21}
365	\]
366	
367	Choose lacunary frequencies
368	\[
369	\lambda_\nu\asymp \eta X^{-a}Y_\nu^{-b},
370	\]
371	with \(\eta>0\) sufficiently small, and let
372	\[
373	F_\nu(t,y)=
374	X^{as}Y_\nu^{-1/p}\,
375	\chi(t)e^{2\pi i\lambda_\nu t}h(y/Y_\nu), \tag{22}
376	\]
377	where the \(y\)-supports are disjoint.
378	
379	For every choice of signs,
380	\[
381	\left\|\sum_\nu\epsilon_\nu F_\nu\right\|_p

25	Write \(J_t^s=(1-\partial_t^2)^{s/2}\). Changes in the Fourier normalization only change constants.

29	### Nondegenerate estimate
30	
31	Suppose \(P\) and an amplitude are supported in fixed bounded coordinate boxes, their sufficiently many derivatives are bounded, and
32	\[
33	|P_{xy}|\geq c>0.
34	\]
35	For
36	\[
37	Tf(t,x)=\int f(t+P(x,y),y)a(x,y)\,dy,
38	\]
39	one has
40	\[
41	\|J_t^\sigma Tf\|_p\lesssim\|f\|_p,
42	\qquad
43	0\leq\sigma\leq\min(1/p,1/p').\tag{2}
44	\]
45	The constants are uniform under the indicated derivative bounds and lower bound. This is the usual nondegenerate Fourier-integral-operator Sobolev estimate.
46	
47	Its elementary, frequency-localized, strict version will also be useful. If \(P_n\) localizes the \(t\)-frequency to size \(2^n\), then, for every
48	\[
49	\theta<\min(1/p,1/p'),
50	\]
51	\[
52	\|TP_n\|_{p\to p}\lesssim (1+2^n)^{-\theta}.\tag{3}
53	\]
54	Indeed, interpolate the \(L^2\) oscillatory-integral bound with the elementary \(L^q\) bound, choosing \(q\) sufficiently close to \(1\) or \(\infty\).

56	### Two-sided finite-type estimate
57	
58	Suppose \(m\geq1\), and on a fixed small coordinate box
59	\[
60	|\partial_x^m P_{xy}|\geq c,\qquad
61	|\partial_y^m P_{xy}|\geq c.
62	\]
63	The planar two-sided finite-type Sobolev theorem gives
64	\[
65	\|J_t^\sigma Tf\|_p\lesssim\|f\|_p \tag{4}
66	\]
67	if
68	\[
69	0\leq\sigma\leq
70	\min\left(\frac1p,\frac1{p'},\frac1{m+2}\right),
71	\]
72	except for the two corner cases
73	\[
74	(\sigma,p)=\left(\frac1{m+2},m+2\right),\qquad
75	\left(\frac1{m+2},\frac{m+2}{m+1}\right).\tag{5}
76	\]
